text:
Your biggest risk is **a shared failure taking out every copy, followed by an unproven recovery path**. Two application replicas can both fail from one bad configuration or simultaneous deployment. The database pair shares an availability zone, and backups have never demonstrated that they can recover orders.

Assumption: acknowledged orders must survive a failure. Streaming replication alone does not establish that guarantee; its acknowledgement settings matter.

With one engineer-week, rank the work this way:

1. **Prove database recovery and identify the order-loss window first.** Restore a recent backup into an isolated database, validate orders and integrity, and measure recovery time. Check replication lag, commit acknowledgement settings, and whether continuous transaction logs support point-in-time recovery. Assign an owner and write the tested recovery procedure. A nightly backup alone can leave nearly a day of orders exposed; even a successful restore cannot recover orders never captured.

2. **Stop changing both application replicas together.** Deploy to one replica, check health and order completion, then proceed to the second; exercise rollback. Apply the same staged approach to configuration changes, with validation and a retained last-known-good version. Confirm that a configuration-store outage lets running replicas continue safely. These changes reduce several likely fleet-wide outage triggers for relatively little effort.

3. **Remove the database’s shared availability-zone failure.** Move the streaming replica to another zone and rehearse promotion and application reconnection, including preventing the old primary from accepting writes. Verify whether replication can lose acknowledged orders during failover. If it can, explicitly choose stronger durability or accept the quantified loss exposure; moving zones alone does not solve it.

Start the restore exercise on day one. At **$20,000 per outage hour**, measured recovery time matters—but irreversible order loss makes the durability check even more urgent. Spend this week proving recovery and separating existing failure domains before adding more copies.
